source_title: Commercial Real Estate Expert Brandon McClain Explains Commercial Real Estate Leasing Considerations in HelloNation
source_excerpt:
MIDLAND, Texas , Oct. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What should businesses evaluate before leasing commercial space? HelloNation published an article answering this question and featuring insights from Brandon McClain of LMB Real Estate Group in Midland, Texas.
The article explains that choosing commercial space involves more than comparing monthly rent. Before signing a commercial lease, businesses should consider whether a property supports daily operations, financial needs, and realistic plans for future growth.
The article addresses location as one of the first factors. Retail businesses may depend on visibility and nearby traffic, while offices and service businesses may value road access and nearby amenities more. The article notes that employee commutes, deliveries, suppliers, and customer access can also influence a location's suitability.
The HelloNation article also recommends examining parking and building access. Delivery areas, elevators, accessibility features, and convenient entrances can affect how well commercial real estate supports normal business activity.
Usable layout is another consideration. The article explains that total square footage does not always reflect how much space a business can use efficiently. Hallways, columns, storage areas, and other building features may limit the available area for employees, equipment, inventory, or customers.
Businesses should also consider future growth before committing to a commercial lease. According to the article, companies expecting additional employees, equipment, inventory, or customer areas should determine whether the property can accommodate those changes. Lease length can become important when business needs may change before an agreement expires.
Building condition may affect both operating expenses and everyday use. The article recommends reviewing heating and cooling systems, electrical capacity, plumbing, roofing, lighting, and internet access. Older systems or deferred maintenance may create costs that are not apparent during an initial property visit.
Commercial Real Estate Expert Brandon McClain is featured as the source of insights for the article's discussion of occupancy costs. The article explains that base rent alone does not show the complete financial commitment. Depending on the lease structure, tenants may also pay taxes, insurance, utilities, common area maintenance, repairs, or other expenses.
Tenant improvements can create additional costs before occupancy. The article notes that businesses may require walls, flooring, signage, electrical work, or other modifications. Lease obligations should identify who pays for these improvements, which changes require approval, and what happens to improvements when the lease ends.
The article also examines renewal options, rent increases, maintenance duties, insurance requirements, signage rules, assignment rights, and early termination provisions. These lease obligations can influence a company's flexibility throughout the agreement.
Zoning and property restrictions also require attention. Businesses should confirm that their planned operations are permitted and determine whether parking, signage, occupancy, or licensing requirements apply. The article explains that this review is especially important when adapting a property for a different use.
The article concludes that evaluating commercial real estate requires businesses to consider the property, occupancy costs, usable layout, tenant improvements, and future growth together. It also notes that commercial real estate professionals can explain market conditions and lease structures, while legal and financial professionals can help review specific obligations.
What Should Businesses Evaluate Before Leasing Commercial Space? This article features insights from Brandon McClain, a commercial real estate expert in Midland, Texas, in HelloNation.
